 Updates as the Proteas host Australia in Gqeberha
 Play starts after rain forces early lunch
 Any thoughts? Get in touch with an email 
 LIVE  Updated  2m ago Geoff Lemon (now) and James Wallace (later) Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.34 EDT First published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT Share Key events 12m ago WICKET! Head b Mulder 121, Australia 209-5 
 1h ago Century! Travis Head 102 from 151 balls 
 2h ago Play gets under way 
 2h ago Lunch taken early 
 3h ago Rain intensifying on final morning 
 5h ago Preamble 
 South Africa's David Bedingham attempts to catch a ball played by Australia's Travis Head.
 Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen South Africa's David Bedingham attempts to catch a ball played by Australia's Travis Head.
 Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty Images Geoff Lemon (now) and James Wallace (later) Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.34 EDT First published on Thu 22 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT Share Key events 12m ago WICKET! Head b Mulder 121, Australia 209-5 
 1h ago Century! Travis Head 102 from 151 balls 
 2h ago Play gets under way 
 2h ago Lunch taken early 
 3h ago Rain intensifying on final morning 
 5h ago Preamble 
 1m ago 07.34 EDT 77th over: Australia 213-5 (Boland 18, Smith 0) Catch down? Kinda sorta. Smith goes get some bat on Mulder’s ball, but with the keeper standing up to the stumps, that hits Rickelton more than being dropped by him. Defensive shot on off stump from Smith, otherwise it was hitting his woodwork, but the outside edge followed.
 Boland has been on 18 for 10 overs. Smith hasn’t scored. There are 58 overs remaining, and three until the new ball.
 Share 4m ago 07.32 EDT 76th over: Australia 213-5 (Boland 18, Smith 0) Boland’s seventh maiden over faced, seeing off Harmer, but the close fielders are getting interested as the odd one turns.
 Share 9m ago 07.26 EDT 75th over: Australia 213-5 (Boland 18, Smith 0) So Head drives a lovely straight four from Mulder, then gets out. Boland survives him, incongruously. Also incongruous is Steve Smith batting at No7 for the first time since 2014. Guess where that happened? Gqeberha. He gets a bumper from Mulder first up, and it goes through the keeper for four byes.
 Share 12m ago 07.24 EDT WICKET! Head b Mulder 121, Australia 209-5
 The man least likely! He’s the understated name in the seam bowling line-up, but Wiaan Mulder has got the biggest wicket! Head chops on again, again, again, even in this innings, even after a ton. Mulder around the wicket, short of a length, angled in, and Head doesn’t need to play this ball, could have dropped his gloves under it, could have let it hit him, anything. Instead, while hopping, he pushes those gloves at the line of the ball, and deflects it down into his stumps.
 South Africa don’t need to wait for the new ball. They’re in.
 Share 18m ago 07.18 EDT 74th over: Australia 205-4 (Head 116, Boland 18) The lesser-spotted defensive Head carries on being spotted, waiting out Harmer’s over before taking a single from the last.
 That is drinks . Australia now with 61 overs left in the day, and 121 runs to make up. South Africa must remain patient and give themselves the chance of a wicket. Everything can change when one falls, and surely at some stage it will.
 Share Updated at  07.29 EDT 20m ago 07.16 EDT 73rd over: Australia 204-4 (Head 116, Boland 18) Head started the day aggressively but has become very quiet in the last few overs. Into a defensive groove. Mulder the bowler, right-arm seam around the wicket to the lefty, who eventually gets a run to fine leg. He’s not blocking bad balls. Boland defends crisply. He’s approaching his Cowan Ton.
 Share Updated at  07.30 EDT 25m ago 07.11 EDT 72nd over: Australia 203-4 (Head 115, Boland 18) Turn from Harmer, but slow turn from the surface. It starts wide and goes wider, and Head can knock it away easily enough. Cuts the next ball for one run to deep cover. Harmer goes up for a bat-pad appeal against Boland, but that ball was all knee-roll, no bat, hitting outside the leg stump. Harmer’s bowling around the wicket to the righty.
 Boland in Test cricket, by the by, has now opened, batted three, and batted five, six, ten, and eleven. Only number four has eluded him in the top six.
 Share 29m ago 07.07 EDT 71st over: Australia 202-4 (Head 114, Boland 18) Second maiden in a row, as Boland blocks out Mulder. Australia remain 124 runs behind in their second innings. New ball nine overs away.
 Share 30m ago 07.06 EDT 70th over: Australia 202-4 (Head 114, Boland 18) Harmer has swapped ends to the one that Rabada was using. A well set field stops Head scoring while playing the ball into the off side. He’s still there at the end of the over though.
 Share Updated at  07.28 EDT 35m ago 07.00 EDT 69th over: Australia 202-4 (Head 114, Boland 18) South Africa will be starting to grind their teeth. That’s 15 overs bowled this morning and still no wicket. Boland is now playing the longest innings of his career to date, 84 balls and counting. Mulder on, almost bowls Boland while leaving, but it doesn’t nip enough.
 Share 38m ago 06.57 EDT 68th over: Australia 201-4 (Head 113, Boland 18) He is up and away! Looks all set to block a sixth maiden over, then from the last ball decides to uppercut Rabada for four instead. Whoosh. Takes the team past 200.
 Share 46m ago 06.50 EDT 67th over: Australia 197-4 (Head 113, Boland 14) For Head, Harmer has a slip, shot leg, and that short mid off, about 20 paces from the bat. A misfield at cover lets Head off strike. Australia 130 behind. Harmer spears down leg to Boland, in between targeting the front pad, and Boland is able to jab one of those leg-stump balls away for a run.
 View image in fullscreen Travis Head plays a shot. Photograph: Themba Hadebe/AP Share Updated at  07.21 EDT 48m ago 06.47 EDT 66th over: Australia 195-4 (Head 112, Boland 13) Looking confident is Boland. Plays a cut shot and an off drive to Rabada, both to the field, but neatly done. Then fiddles at a line tight to the off stump! Nearly nicks it. Defends the next one well off the back foot, ball angled at his body, and calls “No!” stoutly.
 That’s the fifth maiden he’s blocked out. Faced 70 balls so far.
 Share 52m ago 06.43 EDT 65th over: Australia 195-4 (Head 112, Boland 13) Bavuma is riiiiight under the nose on the off side, almost touching the cut strip with his fingers. I think the umpire might even have moved him back a touch the next ball. He’s close enough to get hit by the bat if Boland steps to the off side to drive. But it’s not Boland who is nearly caught by someone close in, it’s Head after gaining strike. Digs out Harmer to a short straight mid on, full ball, and it just bounces in front of the fielder, who doesn’t claim it but the umpires do choose a quick video check.
 Share 1h ago 06.39 EDT 64th over: Australia 192-4 (Head 111, Boland 12) Where’s that come from? Boland has played a back-foot punch off Rabada for four! Not advisable, he saw a few teammates get out yesterday playing that, but on this occasion he times it perfectly and gets away with the decision. Saw a bit of width and went for it, in the same way he got out to Jansen in the first innings, but that time had left-arm angle across, and this time it was going on straight from the right-armer.
 Share 1h ago 06.34 EDT 63rd over: Australia 187-4 (Head 110, Boland 8) Deficit is down to 139. Four catchers around the bat, hoping that the big fast bowler with the blade will take an awkward step and pop up a catch from Harmer off the pad. Short leg, silly mid off, silly point, slip. No leg slip, if Boland gets one off his hip. He’s not going to play an aggressive shot, so why not have that man in? Boland is in the groove now, big step down and defending with the bat angled back, safety first, the b-b-b-b-bomb squad defusing grenades one at a time. So far Harmer’s grenades have been the plastic Halloween type. Tis the season.
 Share 1h ago 06.31 EDT 62nd over: Australia 187-4 (Head 110, Boland 8) Runs keep coming. Rabada is back for Jansen, Bavuma ringing the changes. Not great bowling though. Rabada bowls too short outside off, uppercut for four. Too full and straight, and driven behind point for four. Then outside leg stump, and deflected away for two leg byes. But anyone who’s been to a yard sale knows that if you rummage around in junk for long enough, you can find a gem. Rabada bowls that one, beating outside edge and off stump by a millimetre apiece. Around the wicket to the lefty, a little angle in and seam away, gorgeous stuff.
 Share 1h ago 06.29 EDT 61st over: Australia 177-4 (Head 102, Boland 8) A third maiden blocked out by Boland! He’s stayed out there for seven overs so far today, very useful nightwatch work.
 Share 1h ago 06.27 EDT Technically the stats will say that is Head’s first century away from home. He has the one from the World Test Champs final in London, but that’s counted as neutral. He’s played a few ‘neutral’ Tests, with two finals plus a Pakistan series in the UAE when he started his career.
 I take issue with this kind of stats categorisation. Those performances are still ‘away’ from home, regardless of who you’re playing against. The useful information in cricket is whether the conditions were foreign, more than how well the bowlers knew them.
 Share 1h ago 06.27 EDT Century! Travis Head 102 from 151 balls
 60th over: Australia 177-4 (Head 102, Boland 8) Doesn’t waste any time! Two boundaries in the Jansen over, and Head doesn’t stay in the 90s long enough to be nervous, twice going through the leg side, once fine and once through midwicket. A friendly middle-stump half volley to get your ton? Yes please. Jansen can’t create any pressure.
 That’s a remarkable innings. Fairly restrained by Head’s standards, brisk by anyone else’s, and it has kept his side in the contest. Also a good sign for Australia is that most of his hundreds become pretty big ones, he’s not so inclined as others to reach the mark and get out.
 View image in fullscreen Travis Head raises his bat to celebrate after scoring a century. Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty Images Share Updated at  06.30 EDT 1h ago 06.21 EDT 59th over: Australia 169-4 (Head 94, Boland 8) Harmer, Head. Put them together and you have a shark. South Africa try spin, Australia’s opener adds a single, and there wasn’t much threat in any of that.
 Share 1h ago 06.16 EDT 58th over: Australia 168-4 (Head 93, Boland 8) Australia now 158 runs behind. South Africa won’t worry about that unless it gets down to double figures. And it might not if Jansen keeps bowling like this. Somehow doesn’t get Boland out with a ball that jumps on a middle-stump line, Boland backing away and hauls his bat out of the way as he reads the length. Stumps exposed, but he knew it wasn’t going to hit them. Cool head. He bats out another maiden.
 Share 1h ago 06.14 EDT 57th over: Australia 168-4 (Head 93, Boland 8) Again, a single for Head first ball of the Rabada over, driven to deep cover. They have a sweeper back now. One probably always should for Head. It nearly brings about Boland’s downfall, but instead his nick hits the rope for four. Almost ran the ball away rather than edging it. Why he was running it at first slip, I don’t know, but it somehow bounces and squeezes between the two slippers and away for runs. He even follows up with a single to pinch the strike.
 A few revisions of the equation, I think the target for the day was 82 overs at the beginning, so 79 after this one.
 Share 1h ago 06.09 EDT 56th over: Australia 162-4 (Head 92, Boland 3) Jansen to Boland, who plays him really well. Confidently onto the half-front foot to defend with bat right next to pad whenever the ball is pitched up. Gets hit by a shorter one, glancing blow, and leaves alone what he can. Another over down.
 Share 2h ago 06.05 EDT Play gets under way
 55th over: Australia 162-4 (Head 92, Boland 3) Head is happy to take the single first ball of the day! That’s interesting. He’s batting with the usual No11, Boland was nightwatch last evening, but if they were looking to bat time, then perhaps Boland facing Rabada second ball of the day would not be ideal? I guess it’s also a good thing for Head to play normally and try to score normally, because that’s the way to keep a slight nudge of pressure on the bowlers. Even when runs don’t matter much, they still don’t like strike rotation and being scored from.
 In any case, Boland handles Rabada comfortably, blocking a yorker and then working a run to leg. Head threads his first boundary of the day through point! A bit of a warm-up over from a bowler sending down his 12th of this innings after 12 more in the innings prior.
 Share Updated at  06.15 EDT 2h ago 06.02 EDT Lunch has formally been taken, we have two sessions to play, and they theoretically have determined that 82 overs will be bowled today. That will not happen, one way or the other, but the intention is to play as late as possible, if required. Either that or South Africa kill this contest quickly.
 Share Updated at  06.10 EDT 2h ago 06.00 EDT We are close to action. Sun is out, a little patchy white cloud against the blue sky, and the players are on the field.
 Share 2h ago 05.34 EDT Lunch taken early
 Update: lunch break is taking place now, and play is scheduled to being in 25 minutes.
 Share Updated at  05.40 EDT 2h ago 05.34 EDT “Shame about the rain hope it doesn’t ruin an exciting last day,” writes Tom Barrington. “As a UK based radio cricket enjoyer, I had to find an Australian feed yesterday. I tuned in during the collapse and was amazed at the funereal atmosphere, it really was striking how down the team were and the calls for an enquiry were starting. I think they had a point re Maddinson, but this is still an extremely successful side who have a great chance of winning the series still and ultimately the World Test Championship.
 “Do you think this is part of the difference between the culture around cricket in England compared to Australia (ultimately borne out in results), in the lack of acceptance of failure? I’ve listened to many worse England collapses and there is much more of an acceptance of fate, combined with some gallows humour.”
 In a word, yes. My theory from my experience working a lot in both countries, which others may dispute, is that broadly speaking the English are good losers and bad winners, while Australians are good winners and bad losers. Caveats! Generalisations! Do not deluge me with contrary case studies, I’m talking broad social averages here.
 The theory being that because Australians expect to win, they move on from it quickly and don’t wallow in smug gloating to the same extent, but when their teams lose, they are shocked to the core that such an outrage could happen, and can’t cope with it.
 All out for under a hundred is UNACCEPTABLE to an Australian mind, it is the province of weak teams from weak countries that do not have our indomitable pioneering spirit born of the hardscrabble clay, or something. There’s a lot of hypernationalist myth mixed in there, and a lack of ability to be philosophical about failure.
 But those complaints also have a point, that a lot of flaws in this current team have been visible for a while, and haven’t been addressed, so when a Test falls apart because of those self-same weaknesses, people get stroppy about it.
 Share 2h ago 05.22 EDT “I’m following Australia vs South Africa all the way from Seattle and it’s 2:10 AM. Trust me, there is nothing more Seattle-like than a rain on a weekday. This Test makes me feel included even if I have to sit and wait here at 2 past midnight! On the other hand, the rain reminds me of the South Africa exit in the 1992 world cup against England. Cheers!”
 Not sleeping… in the largest city in Washington state… if only there was a film reference that I could employ. Still, that is serious dedication, Muhammad Najib, to be waiting up all night to read the rain delays. We salute you. Go Orcas.
 Share 3h ago 04.59 EDT Rain intensifying on final morning
 The rain is intensifying. This is settling into becoming a really significant loss of time. On most grounds you’re generally at least an hour from resuming after serious rain, so that would take us past the scheduled lunch break. And on this ground, the outfield got so soaked that we lost several extra hours on day two even in the sunshine.
 Share Updated at  05.25 EDT 3h ago 04.57 EDT “Whilst you’re pondering the weather perhaps you could work on an Edges of Maddinson’s County zinger,” writes Patrick O’Brien. “Actually, does he even use a County? Ah well, carry on.”
 Maddinson uses a DSC. He has played a little bit of county, for Durham. Didn’t go so well.
 Share 3h ago 04.46 EDT “Crisis? What crisis?” asks Rowan Sweeney. “The thing that sets Australian cricket apart is the shared commitment between fans, staff and players to achieve excellence. Case in point - yesterday morning Head and Boland were ready to greet the first ball, and they’re here again for more today.”
 Must be a fairly rare occurrence. I would claim a reasonably advanced stat-search capability, but not sure it’s good enough to look that one up.
 Share 3h ago 04.43 EDT We just did another round of the cover dance. Covers off, revised session times, players warm up, rain returns, covers on.
 Share 3h ago 04.21 EDT “At risk of overcooking the Shield chat,” writes Eamonn Maloney, “you don’t have to select from a bunch of mediocrities averaging 35 when it’s early in the season and the small sample size is inflating averages. Made a big ton? In you go son!”
 If they had more than four days between matches, you might be right, the emergency calls may be going out. Though on the other hand, the current regime is happy to ignore Shield cricket completely when they feel the vibe is more compelling: Maddinson, Connolly.
 Assuming that Green is fit for Cape Town, then somebody has to go: you’d assume Maddinson, Webster, or Labuschagne. And if Inglis is fit and firing, he’s a calm head they they like, so the changes might be dual.
 That said, Labuschagne ‘failing’ in the high 30s is not the worst problem a cricketer can have. And I think they’ve botched Webster’s career by making him peripheral, batting seven and bowling the odd over, rather than backing him at six as part of the top-tier batting unit. He had such a good start but has faded badly in recent matches, and I’d point at least one finger at a lack of clarity about what his job is.
 Share 3h ago 04.16 EDT Scratch that, now the covers are coming back. We’re whittling down the overs that Australia has to face, but the unclear timings would also increase the uncertainty in that dressing room.
 Share 4h ago 04.05 EDT It sounds like we might get play 15 minutes from now.
 Share 4h ago 03.56 EDT Pondering that, there may indeed be some layoffs from this Australian team if they lose here and need to win in Cape Town to take the series.
 I see the Australian team situation as having been the same for a while. A very good bowling attack, whatever their age, but suspect batting. Mostly the bowling is good enough that the batting only has to scrape enough runs together – see Durban, see Mackay. On the occasions when the bowlers don’t dominate, which no group of bowlers always will, the batting can’t cope. See Darwin, see Gqeberha.
 Share 4h ago 03.55 EDT “Our Test team is late-stage capitalism,” writes an unnamed Australian correspondent. “Spurts of comforting nostalgic old reliables coming good (Smith, Lyon, Boland), some new-tech hopes (Head opening), but really we know its allll crumbling. Even the banks are laying off workers.”
 Share 4h ago 03.47 EDT We’re going to have a slightly delayed start because there was some rain this morning. Covers are coming off, at around the scheduled start time. The Australians will of course be very pleased by every over lost.
 View image in fullscreen Covers are on to start day five of the second Test. Photograph: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images/Getty Images Share Updated at  03.50 EDT 4h ago 03.44 EDT You can email me, of course, like Simon D has done: “I’m a pom - living in Aberdeen for my sins - I’m not in the slightest bit bothered about the three way hit and giggle fest going on in Pakistan at the minute. But this... this is gripping. I bloody love Test cricket.”
 That’s the stuff, Simon. Though I will say the concept of an ODI tri-series is now also sufficiently retro that it almost belongs in the same category. Things to please traditionalists. In fact, there are two ODI tri-series happening simultaneously. England and Sri Lanka are in Pakistan, as you say, while Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Zimbabwe are up to the final of their own version in the UAE.
 There’s also an Ireland-Namibia ODI series, India are playing all formats in New Zealand and are halfway through a T20 right now, and Australia’s women are playing New Zealand’s women in a T20 starting any minute.
 But here, we’ve got the real quiz.
 Share 4h ago 03.30 EDT Weather! We’ll have some of it. Allegedly the good kind. Mild day with some sunshine, says the prognostication. Good day for batting, if one can keep at it.
 Early start by 15 minutes, extended finish by “until it gets dark”.
 Share 4h ago 03.10 EDT Want to know what happened on day four of the second Test? Luckily, I know a guy who has a good source for match reports.
 double quotation mark There it was, another entry in Australia’s hall of infamy against South Africa. There was 47 all out, in the innocent days when the 2011 Test was the worst humiliation in Cape Town. There was 85 all out in Hobart, 2016, that led to half the side being sacked. Now there is 99 all out in Gqeberha, one day after the home team blew past 400, only for the visitors to follow on halfway through day four.
 Australia collapse in chaotic fashion to leave South Africa in sight of victory Read more Share 5h ago 03.00 EDT Preamble
 Geoff Lemon What say you, traveller? Tarry by the fire a minute? We may trade tales of desperate glory.
 A bit of that ahead of us today, or at least it needs to be if Australia hope to save this game. This is a team that was forced to follow on yesterday, then lost four more wickets second time around, and they’re still 170 runs behind.
 The equation is this. To take on the task we have Travis Head nearing a hundred, Scott Boland nightwatching at the other end, then it will be Steve Smith with a crook neck, Alex Carey of the horrible shot yesterday, and the bowler trio of Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood.
 Between them, this lot need to bat for three sessions, with perhaps a slightly early end for bad light. Or, if they’re able to score as well as bat time, they could try to make that 170 and get into the lead, where every run is worth double because South Africa would need time to score them back.
 Admittedly that’s unlikely given the four wickets to have fallen, but if things did pan out that way, Australia could kill the game sooner than three sessions by getting far enough in front.
 Far more likely is that South Africa’s bowlers will be refreshed by a night’s sleep, and will pick them off in time, with six wickets to get.
 The series will stay live if South Africa pull this off. High stakes. You in?
